title: Cracked House Walls: Crack Types, Causes and When Dangerous
desc: Hairline, diagonal, horizontal and vertical cracks: how they differ, common causes, signs of dangerous cracks needing inspection, and what owners should do.
summary: How to recognise common types of wall cracks, their causes, signs of danger and the owner's responsibility when a work is at risk of being unsafe.
body: p

Almost every house develops cracks after a few years. Some are merely cracks in the plaster that are fixed by repainting; others are signs of foundation settlement or a problem in the load-bearing structure. Knowing the difference spares you needless worry, and also stops you ignoring a real risk.
h2
1. Common types of cracks
ul

Hairline cracks: many small, short cracks interlacing like a spider's web on the plaster. Usually caused by mortar shrinkage, plaster applied too thick or not cured moist. They have little effect on the structure.
Cracks at the junction between a built wall and concrete columns or beams: caused by the two materials expanding and contracting differently and the lack of reinforcing mesh when plastering.
Cracks around doors and windows, often diagonal from the corner of the opening: may be due to a missing or weak lintel (the beam above the opening), or to settlement.
Diagonal cracks in walls, especially on the lower floors and gable walls: a common sign of uneven settlement - one part of the house settling more than the rest.
Horizontal or vertical cracks in beams, columns and slabs (the load-bearing concrete): need to be checked by an engineer.
h2
2. Common causes
ol
Material shrinkage, and plastering not done to the proper technique.
Thermal expansion - west-facing walls, flat roofs without heat insulation.
Foundation settlement due to weak ground, a foundation unsuited to the geology, or neighbouring works excavating foundations or pressing piles.
Extensions, added floors, or knocking through walls that increase the load or reduce load-bearing capacity.
Reinforcement in the concrete rusting from long-term leaks, so the concrete swells and spalls.
h2
3. Signs of dangerous cracks
p
Have a structural engineer or inspection organisation look at it at once if you see any of these signs:
ul
A crack going through the wall, through which light can be seen, or whose two edges are offset.
A crack that grows longer and wider over time.
Cracks in concrete beams, columns or slabs, especially with a sagging slab or spalling concrete exposing rusty reinforcement.
Doors and windows suddenly sticking or hard to open and close; the floor cracking or sinking; the house showing signs of tilting.
Cracks appearing quickly after the neighbouring house is built.
p

A simple way to monitor: mark both ends of the crack, note the date and measure the width; you can stick a thin paper strip across the crack - if the paper tears, the crack is growing. Take photos periodically to compare.
h2
4. The owner's responsibility when a house is at risk of being unsafe
p
Under Clause 1, Article 42 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, when a work is found to be at risk of being unsafe, affecting users, neighbouring works and the community, the owner is responsible for:
ol
Re-checking the existing condition of the work;
Arranging a quality inspection of the work (if necessary);
Taking urgent measures such as restricting use, stopping use, cordoning off the danger zone, and moving people and property if there is a risk of collapse;
Reporting immediately to the nearest local government;
Repairing damage that risks affecting safety, or demolishing if necessary.
p
If the cracks are caused by a neighbouring house being built, see also building a house that causes the neighbour's house to settle and crack: responsibility and compensation.
h2
5. Fixing: only the right cause ends the cracking
p

Plaster cracks can be dealt with by widening, cleaning, filling with an elastic material and repainting. But for cracks caused by settlement or by the structure, filling the surface only hides them temporarily - the cause must be identified and a plan to strengthen the foundation or structure must be calculated by a qualified person. note
